title: Chinese Civil War: mainland-to-Taiwan displacement
description: The Nationalist government, military personnel and civilians relocate or flee from mainland China to Taiwan around 1949. The approximate interval highlights this major phase and its immediate aftermath. Shanghai and Taipei represent one connection; people leave from many places and later movements continue. Arrows are schematic links between representative places across this interval, not individual journeys or surveyed routes.

title: Korean War: civilian flight and evacuation
description: War displaces Korean civilians across the peninsula. The December 1950 Hungnam evacuation is one major example of civilians escaping by sea toward southern ports. The line represents that selected evacuation connection, while the viewing interval covers the 1950–1953 war; displacement does not end with the armistice. Arrows are schematic links between representative places across this interval, not individual journeys or surveyed routes.

title: Hungarian Revolution: refugee flight
description: The suppression of the 1956 Hungarian uprising drives refugees into Austria and Yugoslavia. Many subsequently resettle elsewhere, while some return. Budapest represents an origin region and the arrows show two selected directions of escape; they do not assign the same route or political identity to every refugee. Arrows are schematic links between representative places across this interval, not individual journeys or surveyed routes.

title: Vietnam War aftermath: Vietnamese refugee departures
description: After the Vietnam War, people leave Viet Nam by sea and other routes amid political persecution, hardship and regional conflict. Malaysia and Hong Kong represent first-asylum destinations, followed in many cases by resettlement elsewhere. The 1996 cutoff marks the formal end of the regional Comprehensive Plan of Action, not the end of Vietnamese migration. Arrows are schematic links between representative places across this interval, not individual journeys or surveyed routes.

title: Soviet–Afghan War: refugees in Pakistan and Iran
description: War and repression drive Afghans into Pakistan, Iran and other countries. Flight begins before the Soviet invasion and continues after the Soviet withdrawal. The 1979–1989 interval highlights the Soviet-war phase; the Kabul marker and two arrows represent selected connections rather than all origins or border crossings. Arrows are schematic links between representative places across this interval, not individual journeys or surveyed routes.

title: Bosnian War: refugees and internal displacement
description: War, ethnic cleansing and persecution uproot people across Bosnia and Herzegovina. Some seek refuge in neighbouring countries or farther away; others remain displaced within Bosnia. Sarajevo represents an affected city. The lines show selected outward connections, and the war-end cutoff does not imply that refugees have returned. Arrows are schematic links between representative places across this interval, not individual journeys or surveyed routes.

title: Rwandan genocide and war: regional refugee crisis
description: The genocide against the Tutsi and armed conflict cause mass displacement within Rwanda and across its borders. Refugees flee toward Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Tanzania, among other destinations. The interval highlights the 1994 exodus and major 1996 returns; people’s circumstances and later movements vary. Arrows are schematic links between representative places across this interval, not individual journeys or surveyed routes.

title: Syrian war: refugee displacement and continuing exile
description: Conflict from 2011 forces Syrians to seek safety within the country and abroad, including in Lebanon, Türkiye and Jordan. Refugees and returnees continue to need protection after later political changes. These outward arrows summarise selected displacement connections; they do not depict current traffic or return flows. The 2026 endpoint is the atlas coverage limit. Arrows are schematic links between representative places across this interval, not individual journeys or surveyed routes.

title: Russia’s full-scale invasion: flight from Ukraine
description: Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022 causes major new displacement in Ukraine and across its borders, intensifying a crisis already under way since 2014. The arrows show selected routes toward Poland and Moldova, not all destinations or present-day traffic. Refugees and displaced people remain in need of protection; 2026 is the atlas coverage limit. Arrows are schematic links between representative places across this interval, not individual journeys or surveyed routes.

title: Belarus after 2020: political exile in Poland
description: Repression following Belarus’s 2020 presidential election drives people to seek safety in Poland, alongside migration for other reasons. Not every Belarusian resident in Poland is a political exile or has refugee status. The Minsk–Poland connection summarises this continuing displacement phase through the atlas’s 2026 coverage limit; it is not a picture of present-day traffic. Arrows are schematic links between representative places across this interval, not individual journeys or surveyed routes.

title: Jewish escape from Nazi persecution
description: Nazi persecution drives Jews to seek refuge from Germany and later from German-occupied Europe. Admission restrictions and tightening Nazi controls leave many unable to escape. Berlin–France and Vienna–Switzerland represent selected directions of refuge across the period; they do not imply a safe or continuously open passage. Wartime deportation and postwar resettlement have separate records. Arrows are schematic links between representative places across this interval, not individual journeys or surveyed routes.

title: Kindertransport: refugee children escape to Britain
description: Rescue efforts bring predominantly Jewish children from Nazi-controlled territory to Britain, usually without their parents. Most transports take place before World War II begins; the broader 1938–1940 chronology includes the final escape from the Netherlands. The line represents a selected Germany–Netherlands–Harwich–London connection, not every child’s journey. Arrows are schematic links between representative places across this interval, not individual journeys or surveyed routes.

title: Holocaust: forced deportations to killing centres
description: Nazi authorities forcibly deport Jews to killing centres as part of the genocide. The Drancy–Auschwitz-Birkenau and Warsaw–Treblinka lines represent selected deportation connections during the main mass-deportation phase of 1942–1944. These are transports to persecution and murder, not refugee escape. Deportation and forced marches also occur outside this selected interval. Arrows are schematic links between representative places across this interval, not individual journeys or surveyed routes.

title: Pale of Settlement: Jewish residency restrictions
description: From 1791, the Russian Empire confines most Jewish permanent residence to a changing western region. Boundaries, exemptions and restrictions within the Pale vary over time; it is not an independent state. Wartime measures weaken the restrictions before their legal abolition by the Provisional Government in 1917. The Mogilev marker identifies one community associated with the Pale, rather than outlining its full extent. This entry supplies residency-policy context for Jewish migration; it does not depict a migration journey.

title: Egyptian marriage contract records financial protections
description: A surviving marriage contract from Asyut sets out payments and property arrangements in the event of divorce. It is evidence for particular legal protections in Ptolemaic Egypt, not the beginning of women’s rights or proof of equality for every woman.

title: Magna Carta addresses widows’ property and remarriage
description: Clauses 7 and 8 of the 1215 charter address a widow’s inheritance and protection against forced remarriage. A widow holding land still needs the king’s or her lord’s consent to remarry. These limited feudal protections are not universal women’s rights.

title: Christine de Pizan writes The Book of the City of Ladies
description: Around 1405, Christine de Pizan constructs a literary defence of women against hostile stereotypes. The book presents women’s intellectual and moral capabilities; its publication is an advocacy milestone, not a change in law.

title: Olympe de Gouges demands equal citizenship for women
description: Olympe de Gouges publishes the Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen, demanding political and civil equality. This is a demand for rights, not an enacted grant of suffrage.

title: Mary Wollstonecraft argues for women’s equal education
description: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman argues that women should receive an education that develops their reason and independence. The book is an influential intervention in debates about equality, rather than a law opening schools.

title: Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule open a girls’ school in Pune
description: Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule establish a school for girls in Pune. Their work challenges exclusion from education. This entry identifies the documented school milestone without claiming that girls’ education began there or that schooling became universally accessible.

title: Seneca Falls convention adopts the Declaration of Sentiments
description: Participants at the Seneca Falls convention call for women’s civil, social and political rights, including voting. The convention is a US organizing milestone, not the beginning of women’s struggles worldwide or the achievement of the rights demanded.

title: University of London opens its degrees to women
description: A supplemental charter makes University of London degrees available to women on the same academic terms as men. This changes access at this university, not at every British institution or for all women in practice.

title: Married women gain wider control of property under English law
description: The Married Women’s Property Act 1882 expands married women’s capacity to hold and dispose of their own property under the law of England, Wales and Ireland. It takes effect in 1883. Scotland has a separate legal history; the Act does not establish complete equality.

title: Tsuda Umeko establishes a higher-education school for women
description: Tsuda Umeko founds Joshi Eigaku Juku in Tokyo, one of Japan’s early private institutions of higher education for women. The school expands educational opportunities without representing universal admission or the first education of Japanese women.

title: Australian federal suffrage expands with racial exclusions
description: The Commonwealth Franchise Act allows eligible women to vote and stand for federal parliament. It excludes many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and people classified by the law as natives of Africa, Asia or Pacific islands, with limited exceptions. This is not universal suffrage.

title: Finland grants women the vote and eligibility for parliament
description: The parliamentary reform of 1906 gives women voting rights and the right to stand for election in the Grand Duchy of Finland. Nineteen women are elected in 1907. Voting rights should be distinguished from equal representation in office.

title: Britain grants parliamentary votes to some women
description: The Representation of the People Act enfranchises women aged 30 and over who meet its qualifying conditions. Most younger adult women remain excluded. The same-year reform allowing women to stand for Parliament is distinct; equal voting terms follow in 1928.

title: The US Nineteenth Amendment bars sex-based voting exclusion
description: Ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment prohibits denying citizens the vote on account of sex. Racial discrimination, citizenship exclusions and other barriers continue to obstruct many Black, Indigenous, Asian American and other women. The amendment does not give every woman an effective vote immediately.

title: Britain establishes equal voting terms for women and men
description: The Equal Franchise Act gives women the parliamentary vote on the same age terms as men, at 21. This removes the sex-based age distinction left by the 1918 reform; it is a franchise milestone rather than proof of equality in every area of life.

title: Ecuador’s constitution recognizes women’s voting rights
description: The 1929 constitution formally recognizes women’s voting rights in Ecuador. Literacy requirements still exclude many people. The milestone follows Matilde Hidalgo’s exercise of the vote in 1924, rather than marking the first time any Ecuadorian woman voted.

title: Brazil’s electoral code recognizes women as voters
description: The 1932 electoral code recognizes women’s right to vote and stand for election. Literacy and other electoral restrictions still limit participation. National political rights develop unevenly after the code; this is not a claim that every Brazilian woman can vote in 1932.

title: Türkiye grants women parliamentary voting and candidacy rights
description: Constitutional and electoral changes in December 1934 give women the right to vote and stand in national parliamentary elections. Earlier municipal reforms preceded this step. The Ankara point represents the national legislative milestone.

title: France recognizes women’s right to vote and stand for election
description: The ordinance of 21 April 1944 recognizes women as electors and candidates on the same terms as men. French women first vote under the reform in 1945. The measure is issued in Algiers; colonial exclusions have their own later history.

title: Japan’s electoral reform enfranchises women
description: A postwar revision of Japan’s electoral law recognizes women’s right to vote. Women participate in the 1946 general election. The milestone records a change in political rights, not the end of other legal or social inequalities.

title: India’s constitution establishes universal adult suffrage
description: The Constitution establishes universal adult suffrage, replacing the restricted franchise inherited from colonial rule. Women vote in the first general election of 1951–1952. Limited voting rights existed before independence, so 1950 is not the first vote by any Indian woman.

title: Egypt recognizes women’s national political rights
description: Egypt’s 1956 reforms recognize women’s rights to vote and stand for election. Women enter parliament in 1957. Legal recognition is a milestone in a longer struggle, rather than proof that all barriers to participation disappear.

title: Tunisia adopts the Code of Personal Status
description: Promulgated in August 1956 and effective in January 1957, Tunisia’s Code of Personal Status changes marriage and divorce law, including prohibiting polygamy and establishing judicial divorce. It is a significant reform, not complete legal equality between women and men.

title: South African women march against apartheid pass laws
description: On 9 August, about 20,000 women march to Pretoria’s Union Buildings to oppose the extension of pass controls to women. Their protest connects women’s organizing with resistance to apartheid. The march itself does not repeal the pass-law system.

title: The UN adopts CEDAW, the women’s rights convention
description: The UN General Assembly adopts the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women. It addresses discrimination in public and private life and enters into force in 1981. Adoption does not mean every country ratifies it or immediately implements its obligations.

title: The Belém do Pará Convention addresses violence against women
description: The Organization of American States adopts a convention recognizing women’s right to live free from violence and setting obligations for states parties. The treaty covers public and private violence. Adoption is distinct from ratification and effective protection in each country.

title: The Beijing conference adopts a global platform for women’s rights
description: The Fourth World Conference on Women adopts the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, setting an agenda across areas including education, health, violence and political participation. It is an international policy commitment, not a law immediately granting identical rights everywhere.

title: UN resolution 1325 recognizes women’s role in peace and security
description: The Security Council adopts resolution 1325 on women, peace and security. It calls for women’s participation in peace processes and protection of women and girls in armed conflict. This is a framework for action, not evidence that conflicts or exclusion end.

title: The African Union adopts the Maputo Protocol
description: Adopted in Maputo, the protocol addresses women’s equality, freedom from violence and reproductive rights. Article 14 includes abortion on specified grounds, including sexual assault, rape, incest and threats to health or life. Treaty obligations depend on participation and implementation; adoption does not change every national law at once.

title: Ellen Johnson Sirleaf takes office as Liberia’s president
description: On 16 January, Ellen Johnson Sirleaf is inaugurated as Liberia’s president, becoming Africa’s first elected woman head of state. Her presidency is a representation milestone, not a claim that women’s political or social equality has been achieved.

title: Kenya enacts the Prohibition of Female Genital Mutilation Act
description: Kenya enacts a specific law prohibiting female genital mutilation and related conduct. The milestone records a legislative measure against a harmful practice; it does not imply that the practice or barriers to protection immediately disappear.

title: Saudi Arabia lifts the ban on women driving
description: The ban on women driving is lifted in June 2018. The UN Secretary-General welcomes this change. This entry records a specific mobility milestone rather than claiming that wider discrimination or restrictions on women’s rights have ended.

title: Taliban authorities exclude women from Afghan universities
description: In December 2022, the Taliban authorities suspend women’s access to universities. The United Nations condemns the decision and calls for its reversal. This records a major restriction on education, not an advance in rights or a claim about every Afghan woman’s experience.

title: Soviet Russia permits abortion in public hospitals
description: Soviet Russia legalizes abortion in 1920 within a public medical framework. This is a major early legal change, not a guarantee of unrestricted or equal access. The policy is reversed in 1936, and abortion is re-legalized in the Soviet Union in 1955.

title: The Soviet government severely restricts abortion
description: The Soviet government prohibits most abortions in 1936, retaining narrow medical exceptions. This reverses the 1920 policy and is part of a broader intervention in family and reproductive life. The restriction is a historical setback, with re-legalization following in 1955.

title: The Soviet Union re-legalizes abortion
description: The Soviet Union re-legalizes abortion in 1955 after the restrictive 1936 policy. Legal provision, medical capacity and contraceptive access remain different questions. This is a dated Soviet policy change, not a statement of the laws of later successor states.

title: Britain passes the Abortion Act
description: The Abortion Act 1967 establishes specified grounds under which registered medical practitioners can lawfully terminate pregnancies in England, Wales and Scotland. It comes into force in 1968 and does not extend to Northern Ireland. It is not unrestricted abortion on request.

title: India adopts the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act
description: The Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act creates a legal framework for abortion on specified grounds and subject to medical and procedural conditions. This entry marks enactment in 1971, not unrestricted access or the later amendments to the Act.

title: Roe v. Wade recognizes a US constitutional abortion protection
description: The US Supreme Court recognizes constitutional protection for a decision to terminate pregnancy under the framework set out in Roe v. Wade. This is a historical ruling: the Court overturns Roe and Casey in Dobbs in 2022. The 1973 marker does not describe present law.

title: France enacts the Veil abortion law
description: The law promulgated on 17 January 1975 permits abortion within specified conditions. It is a major reform associated with Simone Veil, rather than unlimited access. Later legislation changes its framework, and a separate constitutional amendment follows in 2024.

title: Canada’s Supreme Court strikes down the abortion provision
description: In R. v. Morgentaler, the Supreme Court of Canada strikes down the Criminal Code abortion provision because its restrictions and procedures violate Charter protections. The decision does not mean that services are immediately available equally throughout Canada.

title: South Africa adopts the Choice on Termination of Pregnancy Act
description: The 1996 Act replaces a restrictive abortion framework with broader access, including termination on request in early pregnancy and specified grounds later. It comes into operation in 1997. Enactment is distinct from the practical availability of services.

title: Nepal reforms its abortion law
description: Nepal’s 2002 legal reform permits abortion under defined conditions, after a long period of criminalization. Legal change precedes the expansion of approved services. Cost, geography, stigma and information can still obstruct access; the milestone is not a claim of universal provision.

title: Ireland votes to repeal the Eighth Amendment
description: In the May 2018 referendum, voters approve removing the constitutional provision known as the Eighth Amendment and allowing the legislature to regulate termination of pregnancy. The referendum is distinct from the subsequent legislation and the introduction of services.

title: New Zealand adopts abortion law reform
description: The Abortion Legislation Act 2020 reforms New Zealand’s legal framework for abortion and removes abortion from the Crimes Act framework for the pregnant person. It retains statutory conditions for provision. This dated reform should not be read as a statement about every aspect of later access.

title: Argentina’s Congress approves abortion access legislation
description: Congress approves Law 27,610 on 30 December 2020, providing for voluntary termination within a defined gestational limit and specified grounds afterward. Promulgation follows in January 2021. The marker records parliamentary approval, not the date services become uniformly accessible.

title: Mexico’s Supreme Court invalidates Coahuila’s abortion criminalization
description: The Supreme Court invalidates provisions of Coahuila’s penal code criminalizing voluntary abortion and establishes constitutional reasoning against absolute criminalization. This specific judgment is not an identical statutory reform in every Mexican state or proof of uniform service access.

title: Colombia’s Constitutional Court limits abortion criminalization
description: Judgment C-055 of 2022 makes abortion punishable under the challenged provision only after 24 weeks, while preserving the previously recognized exceptions beyond that point. This is a dated constitutional ruling, not a guarantee that barriers to healthcare disappear.

title: Dobbs overturns Roe and Casey’s US abortion protection
description: In Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, the Supreme Court overturns Roe and Casey and holds that the federal Constitution does not confer a right to abortion. The ruling permits divergent state restrictions and protections; it does not itself enact one nationwide abortion ban.

title: France constitutionally guarantees freedom to have an abortion
description: Parliament approves a constitutional amendment in March 2024 guaranteeing freedom to have recourse to abortion under conditions determined by law. The amendment is promulgated on 8 March. This strengthens constitutional protection without making access unconditional.

title: Russian women win voting rights before the Bolshevik takeover
description: Campaigning by women’s organizations helps secure voting rights under the Provisional Government in 1917. Women participate in elections that year, including for the Constituent Assembly. This milestone precedes the Bolshevik seizure of power and is not a claim that political equality is complete.

title: China’s Marriage Law recognizes free choice and easier divorce
description: The 1950 Marriage Law recognizes free choice in marriage and expands access to divorce. It is a major reform of family relations under the new People’s Republic. Enactment and its uneven implementation are different matters; it does not establish complete equality in everyday life.

title: Tunisia broadens legal access to abortion
description: Tunisia’s 1973 reform broadens the grounds for legal abortion after a more limited 1965 change. It permits abortion during the first three months under a medical framework, with specified grounds later. The milestone concerns the historical law, not a guarantee of equal practical access.

title: The US Comstock Act restricts mailing abortion and contraceptive materials
description: Congress enacts the Comstock Act on March 3, restricting the mailing of articles intended for abortion or contraception and associated information. The entry describes the 1873 statute; later amendments and court interpretations change its reach.

description: Colorado reforms its abortion law to permit abortions in specified circumstances, including pregnancies likely to cause the pregnant woman’s death and cases of rape or incest. This is a limited reform before Roe, rather than unrestricted legalization.

title: New York legalizes abortion before Roe
description: New York legalizes abortion in 1970, three years before Roe v. Wade. The reform is a state-law milestone; it does not establish a nationwide right or imply that earlier restrictions and practical barriers immediately disappear everywhere.
